title: the women went first
tomorrow: the rich kid who gave his clothes back

segments.voice: Yesterday: candles, and the Easter flame carried into a dark church. Your line was light a candle for someone. Today, the morning that flame is for. Day sixteen.

Very early on a Sunday morning, near Jerusalem. Jesus has been executed and buried. The men who followed him are nowhere in this scene. A few women are walking to a tomb cut in the rock, carrying spices to anoint a body. That's what you did for someone you loved. On the way, they realize they have a problem. A great stone has been rolled across the entrance. In Mark's Gospel, they ask each other: "Who shall roll us back the stone from the door of the sepulchre?" They go anyway. They don't have a plan. They just go.
screen: `VERY EARLY. A SUNDAY.` → `A FEW WOMEN, WITH SPICES.` → `WHO WILL ROLL BACK THE STONE?`

segments.voice: When they get there, the stone is already rolled away. The tomb is empty. In one telling, two men in shining clothes ask them why they're looking for the living among the dead, and say, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "He is not here, but is risen." Every Gospel tells it a little differently: how many women, how many angels, who sees what first. But all four agree on one thing: women were the first witnesses at the empty tomb. Some scholars point out that a woman's word counted for less in that world, which makes the detail stand out. And the men, one Gospel says, didn't believe them at first: the women's words seemed like idle tales. In another telling, Mary Magdalene stays behind at the tomb, crying, and meets the risen Jesus himself, and doesn't recognize him until he says her name. Then he sends her to tell the others. That's why Catholic tradition calls her the apostle to the apostles: the one sent to the ones who would be sent. Catholics believe the resurrection is the center of everything: that Jesus truly rose from the dead, and that death is not the end of the story. It's why, as day fourteen said, Christians gather on Sunday: every Sunday keeps a little of Easter. Easter itself isn't just one day. It's a season of fifty days, longer than Lent. In Spanish, Italian and French, the feast's name comes from Pascha, the Passover: Pascua, Pasqua, Pâques. And look at the order of that morning. The women worried about the stone the whole way there. By the time they arrived, it had already been moved.
screen: `HE IS NOT HERE, BUT IS RISEN.` · `WOMEN WERE THE FIRST WITNESSES.` · `THE APOSTLE TO THE APOSTLES.` · `FIFTY DAYS, NOT ONE.` · then, large: `THE STONE IS ALREADY MOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one stone you're worried about: something ahead that feels too heavy to move. A conversation, a bill, a diagnosis, a decision. Picture yourself walking toward it anyway, like the women did, without a plan. Breathe slowly as you walk. You don't have to solve it. Just keep walking. If you pray, you can bring it to God.
Easter. The feast of the resurrection, the empty tomb, and the women who were sent to tell. Sixteenth word.
Your line: the stone is already moved. The women only found out because they went anyway. Day sixteen.
